Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-27 14:00 PDT (recorded_at 2026-03-27T21:00:00Z)

Agenda: deep dive on autoscaling, burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPUs for production inference; discuss VPC/on-prem constraints and benchmarking plan
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood), Liam (Nimbus CTO), Jasmin (Nimbus infra), Ravi (Nimbus ML)

Summary (auto):
- Overview of Redwood autoscaling options (reserved pools, burst capacity, queueing) and recommended sizing strategy for low-latency healthcare inference workload.

[00:00] Maya Chen: all right, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. um today Carlos and I will run through the autoscale and capacity planning details, dig into burst policies and some of the queueing tradeoffs.
[00:18] Liam O'Connor: thanks Maya, quick context — we're onboarding a clinical summarization pipeline, so 99th percentile latency needs to stay under 500ms for single-turn prompts and cost sensitivity is high. we also have a big daily spike at 2am UTC.
[00:35] Carlos Ruiz: ok got it, and by 500ms are you measuring from client side or from our API edge? that matters for network time.
[00:44] Jasmin Patel: from client side, includes transit. our infra team will add an edge closer later but for now treat it as end-to-end.
[00:52] Carlos Ruiz: perfect. so we'll talk about tail latency targets, batching, kv cache warmup, and reserved GPU pools.
[01:10] Ravi Shah: one thing — models are 7B quantized, we plan to use KV cache for session-based completions; average output length 120 tokens, input 60 tokens.
[01:25] Carlos Ruiz: great detail, that helps. quantized 7B on A10-ish class GPUs tends to be pretty efficient, but the KV cache will increase memory footprint; that affects how many concurrent sessions per GPU.
[01:42] Maya Chen: high level options: hosted (on-demand), dedicated (reserved GPU pools), private (VPC / on-prem). recommendation for production with strict latency SLOs is Dedicated with some burst capacity and queueing rules.
[02:00] Liam O'Connor: curious on cost tradeoff — how much reserved vs burst makes sense? we expect big spikes but low steady baseline.
[02:10] Carlos Ruiz: typical pattern is reserve for baseline steady qps (say 95th percentile) and allow burst capacity to cover 99.9th percentile peaks; burst is more expensive per-token but avoids constant overpay. but there's a short warmup for new instances that can add 200-800ms depending on model and whether weights are cached.
[02:32] Jasmin Patel: warmup — is that loading model weights into GPU memory or warming KV cache?
[02:38] Carlos Ruiz: both; first is loading model into VRAM and kernel init, second is kv cache warming for repeated session prefixes. the larger latency hit is weight load if the instance wasn't already in the pool.
[02:52] Priya Singh: we have a configurable burst policy — you can set max concurrent burst GPUs, scale window, and a cost limit. you can also pin certain routes to reserved instances to guarantee latency.
[03:08] Liam O'Connor: about queueing models — what do you recommend for requests that want <500ms? drop, queue, or synchronous fallback?
[03:18] Carlos Ruiz: for strict SLOs we usually suggest: route critical routes to reserved instances (no queue), non-critical routes go to a priority queue with short timeout (e.g., 1.2s). we also offer graceful degradation to smaller model variants when capacity constrained — that keeps latency but can affect quality.
[03:36] Ravi Shah: can you run through an example math for queue depth vs latency?
[03:42] Carlos Ruiz: sure. assume per-token service time t_s ~ 3.5ms per token on your quantized 7B and average request 180 tokens total => service time ~630ms per request if served single-request (no batching). with batching you can amortize kernel overhead: batch size 4 might bring per-request to 280-320ms. queueing adds waiting time dependent on arrival rate vs service rate; if arrival spikes to 4x baseline, queue depth grows and P99 latency will exceed SLO even with batching.
[04:20] Jasmin Patel: so batching helps, but increases latency for single request; how do you balance?
[04:26] Carlos Ruiz: we do adaptive batching: short batching windows (10-30ms) and per-route config. latency-sensitive routes get smaller windows, throughput routes get larger ones. plus we have continuous batching where we keep small batches for low latency.
[04:46] [05:00] Maya Chen: note that continuous KV caching reduces compute for repeated prefixes — if your session pattern is many short turns, KV cache can cut per-turn latency by 20-40% after warmup.
[05:16] Liam O'Connor: what's cache eviction behavior? if a GPU restarts, do we lose cache?
[05:22] Carlos Ruiz: yes ephemeral KV cache lives in GPU memory; we persist a lightweight index to control plane for rewarming heuristics but full cache is not persisted across instance termination in Dedicated today — on-prem options can integrate with NVM for longer-lived caches but with tradeoffs.
[05:40] Ravi Shah: you mentioned kernel selection impact — can that cause performance cliff for certain sequence lengths?
[05:46] Carlos Ruiz: absolutely, some attention kernels are optimized for shorter sequences; we auto-select kernels per-request distribution. we recommend profiling your token length distribution — long tails (very long contexts) change capacity needs a lot.
[06:05] Jasmin Patel: on reserved GPUs — how many sessions per GPU should we assume?
[06:11] Carlos Ruiz: depends on model and quantization. for quantized 7B on A10/RTX6000 class, rough ballpark for low-latency single-turn workloads is 20-40 concurrent requests if no batching; with batching and KV cache you can get higher concurrent throughput. we'll send a sizing calc but for your 120/60 token profile I'd ballpark 24 concurrent low-latency sessions per GPU.
[06:36] Liam O'Connor: ok, and burst capacity provisioning timeline — how fast can you add GPUs?
[06:42] Priya Singh: for Dedicated we keep a warm pool for burst; you can configure warm pool size and scaling cooldowns. new cold instances provisioning from cloud can take 2-5 minutes depending on region, but warm pool expansion is near-instant (10-30s) if warm nodes are reserved.
[07:00] Jasmin Patel: is warm pool always charged? how do we manage cost?
[07:05] Maya Chen: warm pool has a lower reserved charge vs fully reserved. we provide a hybrid billing model: reserved commit discounts apply to baseline, warm pool is billed at a fraction and burst usage billed at on-demand. tradeoffs depend on spike frequency.
[07:20] [07:30] Ravi Shah: on the private on-prem side, if we bring our own GPUs, do you support the same autoscaler?
[07:36] Carlos Ruiz: yes, our Private control plane supports a customer-managed cluster with the same autoscale primitives; the difference is provisioning speed — on-prem burst is limited by your hardware. we also integrate with your KMS and private networking.
[07:52] Liam O'Connor: security question — how are logs and audit records handled for Dedicated?
[07:58] Maya Chen: we stream audit logs to your account; for Private we can ship logs to your SIEM. SOC2 details in the security deck I'll send.
[08:10] Jasmin Patel: can you explain the queueing model you use? FIFO, priority preemptive?
[08:16] Carlos Ruiz: it's priority-based queues with preemption options for extreme cases. normal operation is weighted fair queuing across routes; you can set hard caps and timeouts per queue. we also expose metrics for queue depth, wait times, and per-route drop rates.
[08:34] [09:00] Maya Chen: let's walk through a quick sizing scenario with your numbers. Ravi, can you share peak qps and token distribution?
[09:08] Ravi Shah: baseline ~50 qps steady, peaks to 600 qps during the daily spike, average tokens 180, p99 target 500ms.
[09:18] Carlos Ruiz: ok math: required service capacity S = qps * avg service time. if avg service time without batching ~630ms => baseline S = 50 * 0.63 = 31.5 concurrent slots. if we assume 24 concurrent slots per GPU => baseline ~2 GPUs (3 to be safe). peak 600 qps => 600*0.63 = 378 slots => 378/24 ~= 16 GPUs. so you'd reserve for baseline 3 GPUs and rely on burst up to ~16. but that's rough; with batching you can reduce slot time and GPU count.
[09:52] Jasmin Patel: 16 GPUs for peak is a lot overnight; can we instead queue some non-urgent requests?
[09:58] Carlos Ruiz: yes, route non-critical requests to the queue; with a short timeout you might need only 8-10 burst GPUs. also consider using a smaller model variant for fallbacks to lower the GPU requirement.
[10:12] Priya Singh: we'd also recommend a canary route pinned to reserved GPUs for the most critical traffic.
[10:20] [10:30] Liam O'Connor: about burst pricing — is there a cap?
[10:34] Maya Chen: you can set a cost cap per day or per month for burst. if exceeded, the system can block burst or degrade to cheaper model variants.
[10:44] Ravi Shah: can we create custom autoscale rules based on queue length?
[10:50] Carlos Ruiz: yes, autoscale triggers can be CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, or latency SLO breaches. you can compose rules: e.g., scale up when queue depth > 50 for 30s and target GPU utilization > 65%.
[11:05] Jasmin Patel: any guidance for warm-up strategy for KV cache to minimize tail latency at spike start?
[11:11] Carlos Ruiz: pre-warming heuristics: keep a subset of GPUs with replicated session prefixes for top customers, or pre-run synthetic requests that emulate prefixes. we also maintain a lightweight index in control plane to rehydrate caches faster. for your workload, pre-warming top 10% of sessions before spike could cut initial tail latency by ~30-50%.
[11:36] Liam O'Connor: if we do pre-warm, what's the additional memory / compute cost?
[11:41] Carlos Ruiz: memory footprint increases proportional to the number of cached prefixes; CPU/GPU overhead for synthetic warm requests is small but network/IO spikes may happen. we'll detail estimates in the sizing spreadsheet.
[11:56] [12:00] Maya Chen: let's talk SLA behavior during regional outages — do you replicate reserved capacity across regions?
[12:06] Carlos Ruiz: cross-region replication is possible; we support multi-region reserved pools and auto-failover routing. replication for KV cache is more complex; we'd failover to model-only instances in another region and rewarm caches.
[12:22] Jasmin Patel: related, we have data residency rules in EU for some customers — can Dedicated be deployed into EU-only infra?
[12:29] Maya Chen: yes Dedicated and Private options can be region-locked; for Private we can deploy entirely within your VPC/region.
[12:38] Ravi Shah: any special considerations for quantization and autoscaling? will int8 models behave differently during warmup?
[12:46] Carlos Ruiz: quantized models usually have faster inference but kernel selection matters; int8 kernels can require different memory layouts meaning slightly longer cold-start for kernel compile, but run faster once warm. we'll include kernel warmup times in the spreadsheet.
[13:04] Jasmin Patel: can we test using a synthetic load generator that mimics our client patterns?
[13:09] Maya Chen: yes we'll share a load script that simulates your token distributions and session sticky behavior. run it in your environment and in our hosted test to compare.
[13:20] [13:30] Ravi Shah: how do you measure cost per effective inference taking into account warmup and cache misses?
[13:26] Carlos Ruiz: we compute amortized cost: tokens served + instance warmup amortized over expected uptime + cache hit ratio. Redwood Optimize can generate recommendations per-route. you'll get per-route token cost and effective cost per successful request.
[13:46] [14:00] Jasmin Patel: about tooling — what observability will we have during a spike?
[14:02] Priya Singh: Console provides per-route QPS, p50/p95/p99 latency, queue depth, GPU utilization, cache hit ratio, and cost by token. you can set alerts on those metrics.
[14:20] Liam O'Connor: ok let's circle back to the sizing calc output you promised — we'd want conservative, expected, and optimistic scenarios.
[14:27] Carlos Ruiz: yes we'll prepare 3 buckets: baseline reserve, warm pool, and burst headroom with estimated monthly costs.
[14:35] [15:00] Maya Chen: any other technical blockers we should know about?
[15:02] Jasmin Patel: networking — we have strict egress rules, VPC peering needs to be validated.
[15:08] Maya Chen: ok we'll include a VPC checklist and on-prem network requirements.
[15:14] Ravi Shah: on fallback models — can redwood do automated A/B or rollouts when degrading to smaller models to monitor quality impact?
[15:21] Carlos Ruiz: yes rollouts and canarying are built-in; we can route a fraction to fallback models and measure quality regressions via eval hooks or your labeled data.
[15:32] Jasmin Patel: last thing — can we run a 24h benchmark with the same traffic pattern?
[15:36] Maya Chen: absolutely; next steps we'll provide the script and you run it. we'll also run it on Redwood Dedicated to compare.
[15:44] [16:00] Closing recap by Maya:
- Carlos will share capacity-sizing calc and autoscale policy examples.
- Maya will send security deck and pricing template.
- Nimbus to run synthetic benchmark and return peak qps + 99p numbers.
- Follow-up in one week to review results.

[16:30] Meeting ends.
